title: From phantom bulls to ghostly monks: The spooky side of Kent's history
excerpt: A phantom bull, marching Roman soldiers and a mysterious pair of legs feature among six of the lesser known haunted places in Kent
content:
A dripping figure in a castle moat, a phantom bull and marching Roman soldiers feature among Kent’s ghost stories.

If you want to find somewhere spooky to make you jump this Halloween, we’ve taken a look at some places with fascinating ghost stories that you might not be aware of.

Aylesford Priory near Maidstone

Aylesford Priory has welcomed pilgrims for centuries, although its ghost stories suggest some visitors have been reluctant to leave.

At The Friars, as the priory is also known, staff and visitors have reportedly seen an unnamed woman in old-fashioned clothes.

But apparently she is not the only ghost said to haunt the priory.

In his book ‘Haunted Maidstone’, Neil Arnold recounts a legend of a white-robed figure walking with his head lowered.

Two other friars emerge from behind a tree, seize him and drag him towards the priory, before all three disappear.

Arnold also quotes journalist, author and former Kentish Express editor Charles Igglesden, who recounts a legend of a monk punished by being sealed inside a chamber with enough food and water for only a few days.

His remains were supposedly discovered years later and given a burial, bringing the haunting to an end.

Other accounts describe ghostly chanting resembling Gregorian chants, the plainsong associated with medieval monasteries.

Writer and paranormal investigator Neil Nixon suggests the chanting could have an acoustic explanation.

The buildings’ many surfaces, facing in different directions, can reflect and break up sound, which listeners may interpret as voices or singing through a process called auditory pareidolia.

It is similar to looking at a cloud and seeing a shape resembling a face or an animal: the brain recognises something familiar in a random pattern.

Nixon believes hearing stories of ghostly chanting beforehand can influence how visitors interpret the sounds around them.

Old Scotney Castle, Lamberhurst

Don’t let Scotney Castle’s romantic appearance fool you.

According to legend, its moat has an unwelcome visitor: a dripping ghost whose identity depends on which story you believe.

One tale claims former owner Arthur Darrell murdered a revenue officer and disposed of his body in the water.

The officer supposedly emerges from the moat seeking revenge.

Another version identifies the figure as a Jesuit priest who jumped into the moat to escape the authorities.

According to the National Trust, the Catholic Darrell family sheltered Father Richard Blount during the religious persecution which followed the Reformation.

He hid in the castle’s secret priest hole before escaping through the moat under cover of darkness.

Is he now coming back to haunt the place?

Arthur Darrell, the owner mentioned above, also features in another curious tale.

He supposedly faked his death to escape justice, then turned up at his own funeral.

The Kent Archaeological Society recounts how a tall stranger wrapped in a black cloak supposedly appeared at Arthur’s funeral in 1720.

He tapped one of the mourners on the shoulder and said: “That is me they think they are burying.”

He then disappeared.

Many years later, a parish sexton preparing a grave in the church’s Scotney aisle reportedly came across a heavy oak coffin filled with stones.

Was this Arthur Darrell’s coffin? We may never know.

Richborough Roman Fort

Richborough was once a gateway to Roman Britain, and its ghost stories suggest some soldiers are still passing through.

At the Roman fort near Sandwich, hundreds of Roman figures are said to march towards the sea before disappearing.

It seems they are still following an old route, even though the coastline has long since moved.

The site was one of the main entry points for the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43.

It developed into a busy port through which soldiers, goods and travellers passed, linking Roman Britain with the continent.

Paranormal investigator Laura Lumb visited Richborough as the sun was setting and says it was the lives of its former inhabitants that captured her imagination.

“Walking around, I found myself thinking about the people who once lived there, where they would have slept, worked and kept their animals,” she said.

“I could almost hear the murmur of voices and the bustle of a settlement that had once been full of life.

“For me, that is where history and spirituality overlap.

“Standing there, with that sense of connection to the past, I could understand why stories of Roman soldiers walking out to sea continue to fascinate people.

Slough Fort, Allhallows

Slough Fort at Allhallows was built in 1867 to protect the Thames Estuary, and visitors have long reported hearing strange voices and footsteps and seeing unexplained shadows inside.

These reports caught the attention of Kent and South East Paranormal, an investigation team known as KASE, which has visited the fort several times.

During one of its first visits in 2021, team leader Dan Rees filmed inside the lower magazine, where ammunition was once stored.

It was when he later watched those recordings that he noticed something moving past a window.

“When you slow it down, you suddenly realise it looks like a pair of legs,” he said.

“I think that’s the most remarkable thing we’ve captured.”

His colleague Laura Lumb added that the layout outside left the team struggling to explain how anyone could have walked behind the window.

“Outside, there’s a brick wall and no slope, so it’s not as though someone could have been walking uphill behind the window,” she said.

The team returned there on October 11, 2025, when a paranormal app they use produced the name William, prompting members to ask: “Is William here?”

Dan, Laura and fellow investigator Darren reported hearing a male voice reply “Yeah”.

During the same visit, members described feeling touches on their arms and backs and hearing footsteps, shuffling and bangs.

They said some sounds seemed to move away as they approached, giving them the impression they were being led around the room.

St Mary’s Church, Great Chart

St Mary’s Church in Great Chart, near Ashford, has a rather larger visitor in its ghost stories than the usual figure drifting down an aisle.

According to a legend tentatively dated to the 17th century, a phantom bull appeared during a thunderstorm and charged through the church, killing or injuring several people before smashing through part of a wall on its way out.

The Grade I listed church has stood through considerably more than one frightening storm, with its oldest surviving stonework dating from about 1080.

Its striking tower is visible across the surrounding countryside.

In the churchyard, some 18th-century headstones carry carved skulls and hourglasses, reminders that time is passing and life is short.

Theatre Royal, Margate

Margate’s Theatre Royal has stories of a figure watching from a box, an orange light and a scream travelling from backstage towards the stage door.

Built in 1787 in Addington Street, the theatre later came under the management of actress Sarah Thorne, who took over from her father in 1867 and opened a school of acting in 1885.

Sarah died in 1899, although reports from 1918 suggest she may have been reluctant to leave the theatre.

An account reproduced by the Theatre Royal Margate Archive describes sightings of her supposed ghost frightening witnesses enough to call the police.

In January 1966, decorator Alfred Charles Tanner was working overnight when, according to his account, he heard whispers from the stage, approaching footsteps and the box office door slamming.

He also described a heavy thud near the front row, where dust rose as though something had struck the floor.

His experiences were recounted in Raymond Lamont Brown’s 1978 book Phantoms of the Theatre and later reproduced by the theatre’s archive.

The building closed in April 2022, but a £6 million restoration aims to reopen it for the 2027 pantomime season.

Margate paranormal investigator Sean Brady said he had heard stories of a figure apparently jumping from a box above the seats and a Grey Lady haunting the building, while people involved in productions had reportedly found the backstage area “a bit creepy”.

He is now in talks with the council about a possible investigation once the theatre reopens.

Kent residents might want to take extra care on the roads, too, where ghostly figures apparently enjoy hitching a lift and giving unsuspecting drivers a fright.

Online used car retailer cinch found 40 reports linked to Kent when it analysed more than 1,100 entries in the Paranormal Database’s Roads & Motorways archive.

Among the places mentioned is Pluckley, known as the most haunted village in UK.

Reports describe a phantom horse-drawn carriage travelling along the village’s main street.

Other stories include a horse’s shadow appearing beneath a bridge on Bossington Road in Adisham, despite no animal being found when people investigate.

Another spotted figure, beside Broomhill Road in Rusthall, has reportedly caused a driver to stop after believing they had hit a man in a grey suit.

Meanwhile, accounts from the Second World War describe a figure in black armour riding a horse along the A2 between Dartford and Bexley.

All six places feature on the Haunted Directory, an interactive map of 50 locations across Kent created by Kent and South East Paranormal, the investigation team known as KASE.

Each entry explains the story behind the location, whether KASE has investigated it and whether the accounts come from documented reports or folklore, alongside sources and practical information for visitors.

KASE investigator Laura Lumb says the project began as a blog post about 10 locations, but the team wanted to give people more reasons to explore Kent, whether on a day trip or a dog walk.

She said: “It’s not just about the haunted stories and reports. It’s about the history of these places.

“I think nowadays, with technology and with social media, we lose connection to our past, especially with the younger generation.”

The team investigates reports of paranormal activity across Kent and the South East, combining historical research with cameras, sound recorders and equipment that monitors conditions at each location.

Members also produce The KASE Files, a fortnightly podcast exploring ghost stories, local legends and the evidence behind reported experiences.
